tldr: By designing a reward function calculated solely from onboard IMU acceleration without external motion capture or state estimators, humanoid bipedal locomotion was achieved using only 14 minutes of sample collection.
hero_caption: Booster T1 (left) and Unitree G1 (right) obtaining walking policies from only 14 minutes worth of samples with STRIDE. As the foot trajectories show, symmetric and stable bipedal walking patterns emerge in a very short time.
overview:
The dominant approach for acquiring legged robot locomotion via reinforcement learning (RL) is training across thousands of parallel environments in simulation and transferring the policy to the real robot (Sim-to-Real). However, this transfer requires precise robot modeling and extensive domain randomization. One might naturally wonder: why not learn directly on the real robot? Yet for humanoids, two major barriers stand in the way. First, conventional locomotion rewards typically track the base translational velocity, forcing reliance on external motion capture systems or drift-prone state estimators. Second, bipedal locomotion is inherently unstable and prone to falling. It requires vast amounts of trial and error to learn, making hardware damage and manual resets fatal bottlenecks.

To address this, the authors propose STRIDE, an RL framework that functions without any external sensors using only acceleration measurements from an onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of directly tracking velocity, it adopts a dual reward structure: following a target acceleration profile computed from commanded velocity, while maintaining an internal velocity estimate integrated from acceleration. Furthermore, by combining high-gain joint position control (stiff PD control) with left-right symmetry data augmentation, they pushed the sample efficiency of off-policy RL to its limits.

Evaluated in the MuJoCo simulator on two humanoid platforms—Unitree G1 and Booster T1—both robots learned to walk with only 12 to 14 minutes worth of data collection (250k steps). Compared to standard setups, falls during training dropped by 81%, demonstrating that walking can be established quickly while significantly reducing the probability of failure.
contributions: Designed a humanoid locomotion reward that eliminates the need for external motion capture or state estimators and is computed solely from onboard IMU acceleration
Adapted sample-efficient off-policy reinforcement learning (XQC) to humanoids by combining high-gain joint PD control with left-right symmetry data augmentation
Demonstrated in simulation that the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 learn to walk with only 14 minutes worth of data collection, reducing falls during training by 81%

sections.heading: Why is direct locomotion learning so hard on real humanoids?
sections.summary: While training RL directly on real hardware avoids the Sim-to-Real gap, measuring base velocity and managing the inherent risk of falls have been major obstacles for humanoids. STRIDE solves both challenges simultaneously through an IMU acceleration-based reward design and highly efficient learning techniques.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become standard for legged robot locomotion. It usually involves training across massive parallel simulation environments and transferring the policy to the real robot, but this requires accurate system identification models and heavy domain randomization. While quadrupeds have already succeeded in learning to walk directly on hardware within a few minutes of operation, things become much harder when it comes to bipedal humanoids.

There are two main reasons:
- Dependence on velocity measurement: Standard locomotion rewards track the base translational velocity, but measuring this accurately on a standalone robot is difficult. It requires external motion capture or sophisticated state estimators, which suffer from latency, errors, and velocity underestimation.
- Instability of bipedal walking and cost of falls: Bipedal robots are inherently unstable and fall easily, consuming huge amounts of samples before finding a stable gait. Falls on real hardware cause wear and damage, requiring manual resets each time. Minimizing falls is therefore a practical necessity.

To break through these limitations, STRIDE introduces a reward tracking the onboard IMU acceleration profile, alongside stiff joint control and data augmentation. As a result, it establishes walking from just 14 minutes of data in simulation and cuts the number of falls by 81% compared to conventional setups.

sections.heading: Bringing fast quadruped learning techniques to humanoids
sections.summary: On quadruped robots, real-robot learning in minutes has advanced thanks to off-policy RL, symmetry, and gait generators. This paper uniquely adapts those insights to more unstable humanoids while removing the critical assumption of base velocity measurement.
sections.details:
Direct locomotion learning on real hardware has primarily evolved around quadruped robots. Beginning with maximum entropy RL and world models, recent studies using sample-efficient off-policy RL algorithms have shortened training times down to mere minutes.

Behind these efficiency gains were techniques to stabilize Critic (value function) optimization during training and increase the Update-To-Data (UTD) ratio—the number of network updates per collected data point. Researchers also introduced data augmentation leveraging the robot's bilateral symmetry, as well as periodic locomotion priors via CPGs (Central Pattern Generators: oscillators mimicking biological rhythmic movements).

However, these methods assumed inherently stable quadruped robots and relied on base velocity estimators. STRIDE takes a step forward by synthesizing these ideas for structurally unstable humanoids and introducing an acceleration reward that does not depend on base velocity estimates.

sections.heading: Acceleration-based rewards and efficiency-boosting techniques
sections.summary: The authors built a reward function evaluating target acceleration and velocity holding using IMU acceleration measurements and internal integration. Furthermore, setting joint control to high gains (stiff PD control) improves behavioral predictability, which combines with bilateral symmetry data augmentation to achieve dramatic efficiency gains.
sections.details:
The problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The policy $\pi_{\theta}(a_t \mid o_t)$ outputs target positions $a_t$ for the 12 leg joints from observation $o_t$. Observations include joint positions and velocities, previous actions, linear acceleration, angular velocity, and gravity direction from the IMU, as well as commanded, reference, and target accelerations. Neither observations nor rewards contain true base velocity measurements.

### 3.1 Acceleration-Based Reward Design
An IMU cannot measure velocity directly; it outputs base linear acceleration $\alpha_t$. Thus, the method defines a reference velocity $v^{\mathrm{r}}_t$ that approaches the commanded velocity $v^{\mathrm{c}}$ with bounded acceleration, while tracking an internal velocity estimate $\hat{v}_t$ integrated from onboard acceleration. A PI (proportional-integral) control law computes the target acceleration $g_t$ needed to bring the estimate toward the reference. The integral term ensures that target acceleration keeps rising as long as velocity error remains, preventing the robot from staying below the commanded speed.

Because the base accelerates and decelerates with every step in natural walking, enforcing instantaneous tracking hurts gait quality. Therefore, the acceleration reward $r^{\mathrm{acc}}_t$ is computed using filtered values $\bar{\alpha}_t$ and $\bar{g}_t$ passed through a low-pass filter with time constant $\tau=0.25$ s. Standing still yields zero reward, forcing the robot to accelerate to score points. Since acceleration drops to zero at steady-state cruising, a hold reward $r^{\mathrm{hold}}_t$ evaluates the match between estimated and reference velocity. The total reward combines these with fall penalties and regularization terms encouraging upright posture and low yaw rate.

### 3.2 RL Enhancements for Sample Efficiency
To stabilize the humanoid quickly, two key techniques are applied:
- High-gain PD control: Joint PD gains are set high (proportional gain 60, derivative gain 3). Making the joints stiff and well-damped makes the robot's response to commanded target positions predictable, making balance retention vastly easier during early training.
- Left-right symmetry data augmentation: Bipedal walking is bilaterally symmetric. A mirror operator $M$ swaps left and right legs and flips the sign of lateral observations and actions. When sampling transitions $(o_t, a_t, r_t, o_{t+1})$ from the replay buffer, 50% are replaced with mirrored data. This allows learning both left and right steps at once without extra trials.
The algorithm uses XQC, an off-policy method that stabilizes Critic training using batch normalization and weight normalization.

sections.heading: Walking learned in 14 minutes: faster training and drastically fewer falls
sections.summary: Evaluated on Unitree G1 and Booster T1 in the MuJoCo simulator, the robots learned to walk within 12 to 14 minutes across all runs. Compared to standard setups without high gains and symmetry augmentation, training time was drastically cut, and falls during training dropped 81% from over 2,000 to 440.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in the MuJoCo physics simulator using two humanoids: Unitree G1 (a compact humanoid around 130 cm tall) and Booster T1. The 12 leg joints were controlled at 50 Hz, commanding forward walking at 0.5 m/s during 12-second episodes. To mimic real-robot learning, data collection was capped at single-robot throughput (250k transitions, roughly 83 minutes of real time). The success metric was the time required to maintain an average forward velocity above 0.4 m/s and an average episode length above 500 steps over 3 consecutive evaluation intervals.

The results were dramatic:
- Training time: Across all random seeds, STRIDE completely mastered walking with just 12 to 14 minutes of sample collection. The final policy walks stably at 0.48 m/s, completing full episodes.
- Ablation comparisons: Removing symmetry data augmentation extended learning time to 21 minutes on G1 and 18 minutes on T1. Using low-gain control (the default RL-X setting) worsened times to 22 minutes on G1 and 66 minutes on T1. Removing both components resulted in only 50% of runs succeeding within the 83-minute limit, and successful runs took 56 minutes on average.
- Fall reduction: Once walking is learned, the robots rarely fall, meaning 99% of falls happen in the early stage before gait acquisition. By achieving stability early, STRIDE slashed the average number of training falls by 81%, from over 2,000 down to 440.

Additional experiments revealed that increasing the UTD ratio from 2 to 4 improved sample efficiency at the cost of computational load, incorporating a CPG gait prior provided no speedup under high gains and was unnecessary, and training a single shared policy across both robot morphologies suffered from negative transfer.

captions.F1: Booster T1 (left) and Unitree G1 (right) achieving stable walking with the STRIDE policy. As the regular foot trajectories show, both platforms acquire smooth, natural, periodic walking patterns using only 14 minutes of sample data.

sections.heading: A major step toward direct hardware learning and future challenges
sections.summary: STRIDE demonstrates a framework that learns humanoid locomotion in minimal time using only an onboard IMU without external sensors. Future challenges include handling real-world IMU noise and bias, omnidirectional commands, and learning universal policies across multiple platforms.
sections.details:
This study introduced STRIDE, combining a novel reward design based purely on onboard IMU acceleration with high-gain control and left-right symmetry augmentation. It showed that humanoid locomotion learning—which previously had low success rates and took over an hour—can be completed in just ten-odd minutes with high reliability and few falls, building a highly practical foundation for direct on-robot reinforcement learning.

However, the authors point out several limitations and future challenges:
- Sim-to-Real gap (sensor noise): Experiments were conducted in a simulation free of noise and bias. On real hardware, errors in gravity compensation and sensor biases accumulate during integration, raising concerns about drift in the velocity estimate and hold reward.
- Limited locomotion directions: The evaluation was restricted to forward walking (0.5 m/s); extending to omnidirectional velocity commands (turning and lateral walking) is necessary.
- Generalization across multiple robots: Training a single policy simultaneously on G1 and T1 showed no performance gain. Incorporating embodiment-aware architectures that can recognize the robot's physical structure will be important going forward.

takeaways: Replacing base velocity tracking with target acceleration profile tracking plus integrated velocity holding enables locomotion learning without external sensors or estimators
Using high-gain joint PD control in off-policy RL makes action outcomes predictable and significantly suppresses falls in early training
Left-right symmetry data augmentation (mirroring states and actions) is a powerful tool that boosts sample efficiency by roughly 1.5x at zero additional sample cost
Faster learning directly leads to a drastic reduction in falls (81% decrease), which is extremely valuable for hardware protection
limitations: Evaluation remains limited to simulation, leaving the impact of real-world IMU noise and drift on the acceleration-integrated reward unverified
Commands are restricted to straight forward walking (0.5 m/s), without demonstration of omnidirectional walking or flexible acceleration and deceleration
Training a single policy simultaneously on two robot models (G1 and T1) failed to achieve positive transfer with the current architecture, degrading performance
